name: Course Overview
Course Welcome & Syllabus Overview
intro:
Welcome to Physics for Young Scientists!

Physics is the study of how everything in the universe works—from the motion of rollercoasters and race cars to the energy powering stars and the electricity in your smartphone.

Course Roadmap & Units:

  • Unit 1: Motion, Speed & Acceleration — Distance, speed, velocity-time graphs, and freefall.
  • Unit 2: Forces & Newton's Laws — Gravity, friction, inertia, F = ma, and rocket propulsion.
  • Unit 3: Energy, Work & Power — Kinetic and potential energy, conservation of energy, and green power.
  • Unit 4: Waves, Light & Sound — Wave mechanics, sound pitch/echoes, and the electromagnetic spectrum.
  • Unit 5: Electricity & Magnetism — Static charge, Ohm's law, series/parallel circuits, and electromagnets.

Assessment Structure: Each unit includes 3 interactive lessons, 1 auto-graded quiz (50 pts), 1 hands-on engineering assignment (100 pts), and 1 collaborative discussion forum.

name: Unit 1: Motion and Speed
UNIT 1: Motion, Speed & Acceleration — The Science of Moving Objects
intro:
UNIT 1: Motion, Speed & Acceleration — The Science of Moving Objects

Understand scalars vs. vectors, calculate speed and velocity, interpret distance-time and velocity-time graphs, and solve acceleration problems.

Pacing: Weeks 1–3 (Estimated 6–8 study hours)

name: Lesson 1 — Distance, Displacement and Speed
intro:
Learn how physicists describe motion, distinguish between distance and displacement, and master the speed formula.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish between scalar quantities (distance, speed) and vector quantities (displacement, velocity).
  • Calculate average speed using the formula s = d / t and convert between m/s and km/h.
  • Interpret real-world motion scenarios including athletic sprints, cars, and animal speeds.

Lesson Content

Everything in the universe is constantly moving—from the electrons orbiting an atom to the Earth orbiting the Sun. To describe motion precisely, physicists use specific measurements:

1. Distance vs. Displacement

  • Distance (scalar): The total ground covered regardless of direction (e.g., walking 400 m around a running track).
  • Displacement (vector): The straight-line distance from starting point to endpoint with direction (e.g., 0 m if you finish where you started).

2. The Speed Formula

Speed is the rate at which an object covers distance:

Formula: Speed = Distance / Time (s = d / t)
SI Unit: meters per second (m/s) or kilometers per hour (km/h).
Conversion Tip: To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6 (e.g., 72 km/h = 20 m/s).

3. Worked Example

Problem: Usain Bolt ran 100 meters in 9.58 seconds. What was his average speed?

Solution: s = 100 m / 9.58 s = 10.44 m/s (approx. 37.6 km/h).

4. Differentiation & Extension

Support: Use the formula triangle (d on top; s and t on bottom) to rearrange for time (t = d/s) or distance (d = s × t).
Extension: Calculate instantaneous speed vs. average speed on a trip with traffic stops.

name: Lesson 2 — Acceleration and Motion Graphs
intro:
Master acceleration calculations and learn to read distance-time and velocity-time graphs like a data scientist.

Learning Objectives

  • Define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity (a = (v - u) / t).
  • Interpret the slope and area under distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
  • Calculate acceleration, deceleration, and distance traveled from motion graphs.

Lesson Content

When an object speeds up, slows down, or changes direction, it is accelerating. Acceleration measures how quickly velocity changes.

1. The Acceleration Equation

Formula: Acceleration = (Final Velocity - Initial Velocity) / Time
a = (v - u) / t
SI Unit: meters per second squared (m/s²).
Note: A negative acceleration value indicates deceleration (slowing down).

2. Reading Distance-Time (d-t) Graphs

  • Horizontal flat line: Object is stationary (at rest).
  • Straight sloped line: Constant speed (the steeper the line, the faster the speed).
  • Curving upwards: Accelerating (increasing speed).
  • Slope calculation: Slope = Rise / Run = Δd / Δt = Speed.

3. Reading Velocity-Time (v-t) Graphs

  • Horizontal line: Moving at constant velocity (acceleration = 0).
  • Straight upward slope: Uniform acceleration.
  • Downward slope: Uniform deceleration.
  • Area under the graph: Represents the total distance traveled!

4. Worked Example

An electric vehicle accelerates from rest (0 m/s) to 25 m/s in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration?
a = (25 - 0) / 5 = 5 m/s².

name: Lesson 3 — Physics in Action: Rollercoasters and Free Fall
intro:
Explore the physics of theme park rollercoasters, gravitational free fall, and terminal velocity.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain gravitational acceleration (g = 9.8 m/s²) on Earth.
  • Describe terminal velocity in terms of balanced gravitational force and air resistance.
  • Analyze motion changes across loops, drops, and braking sections on a rollercoaster.

Lesson Content

Theme parks are gigantic physics laboratories designed to manipulate human perception of motion and acceleration!

1. Free Fall & Acceleration due to Gravity

When an object falls under the influence of Earth's gravity alone (ignoring air resistance), it accelerates downward at approximately 9.8 m/s² (often rounded to 10 m/s² in introductory physics). This means every second, its downward speed increases by 9.8 m/s!

2. Terminal Velocity

As a skydiver falls:

  1. Initially, gravity is greater than air resistance → the diver accelerates downward.
  2. As speed increases, upward air resistance (drag) increases.
  3. Eventually, upward air drag equals downward gravitational force → net force becomes zero.
  4. The diver falls at a steady maximum speed called terminal velocity (~55 m/s or 200 km/h with a closed posture).

3. Rollercoaster Dynamics

On a drop tower or first drop of a coaster, riders experience near-weightlessness (low g-force), whereas at the bottom of a loop, the track pushes up creating high g-forces (up to 3g–4g).

4. Key Takeaways Checklist

  • ✓ Speed is scalar; Velocity is vector.
  • ✓ Slope of d-t graph = Speed; Slope of v-t graph = Acceleration.
  • ✓ Area under v-t graph = Total distance.

name: Unit 2: Forces and Newton's Laws
UNIT 2: Forces & Newton's Laws — Why Things Move and Stop
intro:
UNIT 2: Forces & Newton's Laws — Why Things Move and Stop

Explore contact vs. non-contact forces, balanced vs. unbalanced forces, friction, gravity, and Newton's Three Laws of Motion.

Pacing: Weeks 4–6 (Estimated 6–8 study hours)

name: Lesson 1 — Types of Forces, Friction and Gravity
intro:
Discover what forces are, how to draw free-body diagrams, and how gravity and friction shape our everyday world.

Learning Objectives

  • Classify forces as contact (friction, tension, normal) or non-contact (gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic).
  • Distinguish between Mass (kg) and Weight (N) using W = m × g.
  • Calculate net force on an object and predict whether its motion will change.

Lesson Content

A force is a push, pull, or twist acting upon an object as a result of its interaction with another object. Forces are vectors (they have both magnitude and direction) and are measured in Newtons (N).

1. Contact vs. Non-Contact Forces

  • Contact Forces: Friction, Normal reaction force, Air resistance/drag, Tension, Applied force.
  • Non-Contact (Field) Forces: Gravitational force, Magnetic force, Electrostatic force.

2. Mass vs. Weight

Mass (m): The amount of matter in an object (measured in kg). Mass NEVER changes regardless of location.
Weight (W): The gravitational pull acting on that mass (measured in N).
Formula: Weight = Mass × Gravitational Field Strength (W = m × g)
On Earth: g ≈ 9.8 N/kg. (A 50 kg student weighs: 50 kg × 9.8 N/kg = 490 N).
On the Moon: g ≈ 1.6 N/kg. (The same student weighs only: 50 kg × 1.6 N/kg = 80 N!).

3. Balanced vs. Unbalanced Forces

  • Balanced Forces (F_net = 0): The object remains at rest OR continues moving at constant velocity.
  • Unbalanced Forces (F_net > 0): The object accelerates in the direction of the net force.

name: Lesson 2 — Newton's 1st and 2nd Laws of Motion
intro:
Unpack the Law of Inertia and the famous equation F = ma that powers modern engineering.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia) and relate inertia to mass.
  • Apply Newton's Second Law (F = ma) to calculate force, mass, or acceleration.
  • Analyze safety features such as seatbelts and airbags using Newton's laws.

Lesson Content

Sir Isaac Newton published his three fundamental laws of motion in 1687, forming the backbone of classical physics.

1. Newton's First Law (The Law of Inertia)

'An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion with the same speed and in the same direction unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force.'

Inertia is the resistance of any physical object to any change in its velocity. The more mass an object has, the greater its inertia! This is why when a bus brakes suddenly, passengers lurch forward—their bodies want to continue moving forward at the previous speed.

2. Newton's Second Law of Motion

The acceleration of an object depends directly upon the net force acting upon it and inversely upon the mass of the object:

Formula: Force = Mass × Acceleration (F = m × a)
Units: Force in Newtons (N), Mass in kilograms (kg), Acceleration in m/s².
(1 Newton = 1 kg·m/s²)

3. Worked Example

Problem: How much force is needed to accelerate a 1,200 kg car at 2.5 m/s²?

Solution: F = m × a = 1200 kg × 2.5 m/s² = 3,000 N.

4. Vehicle Safety Physics

Airbags and seatbelts increase the time duration of a crash. Since F = m × Δv / t, increasing the stopping time significantly reduces the impact force on the passenger's body!

name: Lesson 3 — Newton's 3rd Law and Rocket Propulsion
intro:
Understand action-reaction pairs, recoil, and the incredible physics that sends rockets into space.

Learning Objectives

  • State Newton's Third Law and identify action-reaction force pairs.
  • Explain how rockets propel forward in the vacuum of space.
  • Describe everyday action-reaction pairs (walking, swimming, bird flight).

Lesson Content

Whenever an object exerts a force on a second object, the second object exerts an equal and opposite force on the first.

1. Newton's Third Law (Action & Reaction)

'For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force.'

Important Rule: Action and reaction forces ALWAYS act on different objects, which is why they do not cancel each other out!

2. Everyday Examples

  • Walking: Your foot pushes backward on the ground (Action) → The ground pushes forward on your foot (Reaction).
  • Swimming: Your hands push water backward (Action) → The water pushes your body forward (Reaction).
  • Skateboarding: Stepping forward off a skateboard pushes the skateboard backward.

3. How Rockets Fly in Space

A common myth is that rockets push against the ground or against air to move. In space, there is no air! A rocket engine burns fuel and expels hot gas particles backward at extreme velocity (Action). In reaction, the expelled gas particles exert an equal force forward on the rocket engine (Thrust Reaction), accelerating the spacecraft forward through empty space!

name: Unit 3: Energy and Work
UNIT 3: Energy, Work & Power — The Engine of the Universe
intro:
UNIT 3: Energy, Work & Power — The Engine of the Universe

Calculate Kinetic and Gravitational Potential Energy, apply the Law of Conservation of Energy, and calculate Work and Power in everyday systems.

Pacing: Weeks 7–9 (Estimated 6–8 study hours)

name: Lesson 1 — Forms of Energy, Kinetic and Potential Energy
intro:
Explore mechanical energy forms, master the formulas for KE and GPE, and discover how energy is stored.

Learning Objectives

  • Identify different energy stores (Kinetic, Gravitational, Chemical, Thermal, Elastic, Nuclear).
  • Calculate Gravitational Potential Energy using GPE = m × g × h.
  • Calculate Kinetic Energy using KE = 0.5 × m × v² and analyze how speed affects kinetic energy.

Lesson Content

Energy is defined as the ability or capacity to do work. Energy cannot be seen directly, but we see and feel its effects everywhere. Energy is measured in Joules (J).

1. Gravitational Potential Energy (GPE)

GPE is energy stored in an object due to its vertical position or height above ground:

Formula: GPE = Mass × Gravity × Height (GPE = m × g × h)
where m is in kg, g ≈ 9.8 N/kg, and h is height in meters.
Example: A 2 kg book lifted 1.5 m high stores: 2 kg × 9.8 N/kg × 1.5 m = 29.4 J.

2. Kinetic Energy (KE)

Kinetic energy is the energy of a moving object:

Formula: KE = 0.5 × Mass × Velocity² (KE = 1/2 × m × v²)
Crucial Insight: Because velocity is squared, doubling your speed quadruples your kinetic energy! This is why high-speed road collisions are exponentially more dangerous.

3. Worked Example

A 60 kg skateboarder moves at 4 m/s. What is their kinetic energy?
KE = 0.5 × 60 kg × (4 m/s)² = 30 × 16 = 480 Joules.

name: Lesson 2 — The Law of Conservation of Energy
intro:
Learn why energy cannot be created or destroyed, trace energy transformations, and draw Sankey diagrams.

Learning Objectives

  • State the Law of Conservation of Energy.
  • Trace energy transfers in systems like pendulums, skate ramps, and power plants.
  • Distinguish between useful energy output and wasted thermal energy (dissipation).

Lesson Content

1. The Law of Conservation of Energy

'Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another, or transferred from one system to another.'

The total energy of an isolated system always remains constant.

2. The Skate Park & Pendulum Model

  • At the top of the ramp: Height is maximum → GPE is maximum, KE is zero.
  • Halfway down: Half of GPE has converted into KE.
  • At the bottom of the ramp: Height is zero → GPE is zero, KE is maximum (maximum speed!).
  • Total Mechanical Energy = GPE + KE = Constant (ignoring friction).

3. Energy Dissipation & Efficiency

In real-world machines, some energy is always converted into 'wasted' forms (usually heat due to friction and sound). When energy spreads out into the surroundings and becomes less useful, we say it has dissipated.

Efficiency Formula: Efficiency (%) = (Useful Energy Output / Total Energy Input) × 100

name: Lesson 3 — Work, Power and Renewable Energy
intro:
Master the physics definitions of mechanical Work and Power, and analyze how renewable generators produce electricity.

Learning Objectives

  • Calculate mechanical work done using W = F × d.
  • Calculate electrical/mechanical power using P = W / t in Watts.
  • Evaluate renewable energy technologies (hydroelectric, wind, solar) from an energy transfer perspective.

Lesson Content

1. What is 'Work' in Physics?

In physics, Work is done only when a force causes an object to move in the direction of the force:

Formula: Work = Force × Distance (W = F × d)
Unit: 1 Joule (J) = 1 Newton-meter (N·m).
Note: If you push hard against a solid brick wall but it does not move (d = 0), physics says you have done 0 Joules of work on the wall!

2. Power: The Rate of Doing Work

Power measures how fast energy is transferred or how quickly work is done:

Formula: Power = Work / Time = Energy / Time (P = W / t)
Unit: Watts (W) (1 Watt = 1 Joule per second).
Example: A 100 W light bulb transforms 100 Joules of electrical energy into light and heat every single second.

3. Renewable Energy Systems

  • Hydroelectric Dam: GPE of elevated reservoir water → Kinetic energy of flowing water → Mechanical KE of turbine → Electrical energy from generator.
  • Wind Turbines: Kinetic energy of wind → Mechanical rotation of blades → Electrical energy.
  • Solar Photovoltaic: Light energy (photons) → Direct Electrical energy.

name: Unit 4: Waves Light and Sound
UNIT 4: Waves, Light & Sound — Energy in Motion
intro:
UNIT 4: Waves, Light & Sound — Energy in Motion

Investigate transverse vs. longitudinal waves, the wave speed equation, the physics of sound and pitch, and the behavior of light across the electromagnetic spectrum.

Pacing: Weeks 10–12 (Estimated 6–8 study hours)

name: Lesson 1 — Anatomy and Properties of Waves
intro:
Discover how waves transfer energy without transferring matter, and master the wave speed equation v = f × λ.

Learning Objectives

  • Compare transverse waves (light, water) and longitudinal waves (sound, seismic P-waves).
  • Define and identify wavelength (λ), frequency (f), amplitude, period (T), crest, and trough.
  • Use the wave speed equation (v = f × λ) to calculate speed, frequency, or wavelength.

Lesson Content

A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another through oscillations, without transferring matter itself.

1. Transverse vs. Longitudinal Waves

  • Transverse Waves: Particles oscillate perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of wave travel. Examples: Light, ocean surface ripples, radio waves. Features: Crests (peaks) and Troughs (valleys).
  • Longitudinal Waves: Particles oscillate parallel (back and forth) to the direction of wave travel. Example: Sound waves. Features: Compressions (bunged together) and Rarefactions (spread apart).

2. Key Wave Parameters

  • Wavelength (λ): Distance between two identical consecutive points (e.g., crest to crest), measured in meters (m).
  • Frequency (f): The number of complete waves passing a fixed point per second, measured in Hertz (Hz).
  • Amplitude: Maximum displacement from equilibrium (rest position). Related directly to energy!
  • Period (T): Time for one complete wave cycle: T = 1 / f.

3. The Wave Equation

Formula: Wave Speed = Frequency × Wavelength (v = f × λ)
Units: Speed in m/s, Frequency in Hz, Wavelength in m.

4. Worked Example

A radio station broadcasts an FM wave with a frequency of 100 MHz (100,000,000 Hz). If radio waves travel at the speed of light (300,000,000 m/s), what is the wavelength?
λ = v / f = (300,000,000 m/s) / (100,000,000 Hz) = 3.0 meters.

name: Lesson 2 — Sound Waves, Pitch and Acoustics
intro:
Explore sound propagation, how amplitude controls volume, frequency controls pitch, and the physics of echoes.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why sound requires a physical medium and cannot travel through a vacuum.
  • Relate wave amplitude to loudness (decibels) and frequency to musical pitch.
  • Calculate distance using the speed of sound and echo reflection (d = (v × t) / 2).

Lesson Content

1. How Sound Travels

Sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects. Because sound relies on colliding particles to transmit its vibrations, sound CANNOT travel through a vacuum (empty space). Sci-Fi space explosions with loud booming noises are physically impossible!

2. Speed of Sound in Different Media

  • Air (at 20°C): ~343 m/s (~1,235 km/h).
  • Water: ~1,480 m/s (over 4 times faster than in air!).
  • Steel / Solids: ~5,000 m/s (particles are packed tightly together, transferring kinetic vibrations rapidly).

3. Pitch vs. Volume

  • Pitch: Determined by frequency. High frequency = High pitch (e.g., whistle); Low frequency = Deep bass (e.g., tuba). Humans can hear between 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz.
  • Volume (Loudness): Determined by amplitude. Larger amplitude = Louder sound (measured in decibels, dB).

4. Echoes and Echolocation (Sonar)

An echo is a reflected sound wave. To find distance to a wall or ocean floor:
Distance = (Speed of Sound × Total Echo Time) / 2 (divided by 2 because the sound travels there and back!).

name: Lesson 3 — Light, Reflection, Refraction & the EM Spectrum
intro:
Explore the speed of light, law of reflection, refraction through lenses, and the full electromagnetic spectrum.

Learning Objectives

  • State the Law of Reflection and explain image formation in plane mirrors.
  • Explain refraction as the bending of light caused by a change in speed across different optical media.
  • Arrange the electromagnetic spectrum from lowest frequency (radio) to highest frequency (gamma rays).

Lesson Content

1. The Nature of Light

Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave that can travel through empty space at the ultimate cosmic speed limit: c = 300,000,000 m/s (3 × 10⁸ m/s).

2. Reflection and Refraction

  • Law of Reflection: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (θ_i = θ_r), measured relative to the normal line.
  • Refraction: When light passes from one medium to another (e.g., from air into water or glass), it changes speed and bends. Moving into a denser medium slows the light down, bending it towards the normal.

3. The Electromagnetic (EM) Spectrum

From longest wavelength / lowest energy to shortest wavelength / highest energy:

  1. Radio Waves: Broadcasting and telecommunications.
  2. Microwaves: Cooking food, Wi-Fi, satellite GPS.
  3. Infrared (IR): Thermal imaging, remote controls, radiant heat.
  4. Visible Light: Red (longest λ) to Violet (shortest λ) — the only band human eyes detect!
  5. Ultraviolet (UV): Suntans, sterilization, causes sunburns.
  6. X-rays: Medical bone imaging, airport luggage security.
  7. Gamma Rays: High-energy radiation from nuclear reactions, cancer radiotherapy.

name: Unit 5: Electricity and Magnetism
UNIT 5: Electricity & Magnetism — Circuits and Modern Power
intro:
UNIT 5: Electricity & Magnetism — Circuits and Modern Power

Understand electric charge, solve circuit problems with Ohm's Law (V = IR), compare series vs. parallel circuits, and explore electromagnets and motors.

Pacing: Weeks 13–15 (Estimated 6–8 study hours)

name: Lesson 1 — Electric Charge and Static Electricity
intro:
Learn about atomic charges, electron transfer, electrostatic attraction/repulsion, and lightning safety.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain electric charge in terms of protons (+), electrons (-), and charge conservation.
  • State the Law of Electrostatic Attraction and Repulsion.
  • Describe real-world electrostatic phenomena (balloon rub, photocopiers, lightning discharge).

Lesson Content

All matter is made of atoms containing positively charged protons, neutral neutrons, and negatively charged electrons. Electricity is the movement and interaction of these electric charges.

1. The Law of Electric Charges

  • Like charges repel (+ and + repel, - and - repel).
  • Opposite charges attract (+ and - attract each other).

2. Static Electricity: Friction and Charge Transfer

When two insulating materials are rubbed together (e.g., rubbing a rubber balloon on a wool sweater), friction transfers electrons from one material to the other:

  • The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged.
  • The material that loses electrons is left with an excess of protons and becomes positively charged.
  • Note: Protons are trapped tightly inside atomic nuclei—only electrons move!

3. Lightning: Nature's Ultimate Static Discharge

In a thundercloud, violent collisions between ice particles cause massive charge separation (negative charges accumulate at the base of the cloud). When the voltage potential becomes enormous, electrons ionize the air and discharge violently to the ground as a bolt of lightning, carrying up to 30,000 Amperes of current!

name: Lesson 2 — Current, Voltage, Resistance and Ohm's Law
intro:
Master the fundamental triumvirate of electric circuits: Current (I), Voltage (V), Resistance (R), and Ohm's Law.

Learning Objectives

  • Define Current (I) in Amperes, Potential Difference / Voltage (V) in Volts, and Resistance (R) in Ohms.
  • Apply Ohm's Law (V = I × R) to calculate voltage, current, or resistance in electric circuits.
  • Use circuit symbols to draw and interpret schematic circuit diagrams.

Lesson Content

1. The Three Key Circuit Quantities

  • Current (I): The rate of flow of electric charge (electrons). Measured in Amperes (A) with an Ammeter connected in series.
  • Voltage (V) / Potential Difference: The electrical push or energy provided per unit charge by the battery. Measured in Volts (V) with a Voltmeter connected in parallel.
  • Resistance (R): How much a component opposes the flow of electric current. Measured in Ohms (Ω).

2. Ohm's Law

Formula: Voltage = Current × Resistance (V = I × R)
Rearranged: I = V / R and R = V / I.
Physical Meaning: If you increase voltage, current increases. If you increase resistance, current decreases!

3. Worked Example

Problem: A smartphone charger produces a voltage of 5.0 V connected to an internal circuit with a resistance of 2.5 Ω. How much current flows?

Solution: I = V / R = 5.0 V / 2.5 Ω = 2.0 Amperes.

4. Electrical Power in Circuits

Electrical Power = Voltage × Current (P = V × I)

name: Lesson 3 — Series vs. Parallel Circuits and Electromagnetism
intro:
Compare series and parallel circuit behavior, understand household wiring safety, and discover electromagnets and electric motors.

Learning Objectives

  • Contrast series circuits (single loop) with parallel circuits (branching paths).
  • Explain why household appliances are wired in parallel rather than series.
  • Describe how an electric current creates a magnetic field, and how to build a powerful electromagnet.

Lesson Content

1. Series vs. Parallel Circuits

FeatureSeries CircuitParallel Circuit
PathwaysSingle continuous loop for all charges.Multiple independent branches.
If one bulb breaksALL bulbs turn off (circuit is broken).Other branches remain lit and working!
Current (I)Same current everywhere: I_total = I_1 = I_2.Current splits across branches: I_total = I_1 + I_2.
Voltage (V)Voltage splits: V_total = V_1 + V_2.Full voltage across every branch: V_total = V_1 = V_2.
Household UseOld holiday string lights.Standard home wiring!

2. Electromagnetism: Magnets from Electricity

When an electric current flows through a wire, it generates a circular magnetic field around the wire. By coiling the wire tightly around an iron nail (forming a solenoid), you create a controllable Electromagnet!

3. How to Make an Electromagnet Stronger

  1. Increase the number of wire coils/turns.
  2. Increase the electric current (higher voltage battery).
  3. Use a soft ferromagnetic core (like an iron nail).

4. Everyday Applications

Electromagnets power electric vehicle motors, Maglev bullet trains, MRI scanners in hospitals, and giant scrapyard lifting cranes!

name: Unit 5 Assignment — Smart Home Circuit Architecture & Safety Blueprint
intro:
Design Challenge: You are the chief electrical engineer designing the circuitry and safety systems for an eco-friendly modern smart home.

Blueprint Specifications:

  1. Circuit Schematic: Draw a clean circuit diagram containing:
    • A 120 V main power source.
    • At least three separate parallel branches: (1) Living room lighting, (2) Kitchen high-power appliances, (3) Bedroom smart devices.
    • Individual switches for each room and a master fuse / circuit breaker in the main branch.
  2. Circuit Calculations (V = IR and P = VI):
    • If Branch 1 has two 60 W lamps operating at 120 V, calculate the current drawn by each lamp.
    • If a 1,200 W microwave in Branch 2 operates at 120 V, calculate its current and electrical resistance.
    • Calculate total current drawn when all devices run simultaneously. What rating fuse (e.g., 10 A, 15 A, 20 A) should be installed?
  3. Safety & Electromagnet Analysis: Explain how an electromagnetic circuit breaker automatically trips to prevent house fires during an electrical overload.
